title: Mastercard Max Launches As AI-Powered Card Benefits Assistant For Asia Pacific Issuers
excerpt: . Mastercard has introduced Mastercard Max, an AI-powered “Benefits Assistant” now available globally, designed to help cardholders across Asia Pacific discover and use their card benefits more effectively. The tool is embedded directly into issuers’ digital channels, allowing cardholders to find relevant benefits tailored to their card, eligibility, location and context, without having to dig through separate apps or documentation. How Mastercard Max Works. Mastercard Max uses conversational AI (it’s 2026, chatbot’s all the craze after all) combined with benefit content sourced from Mastercard and participating issuers. Cardholders can ask questions in natural language and receive answers specific to their card and situation. As an example, a cardholder planning a trip could use the assistant to identify available travel benefits, receive reminders about airport lounge access on the way to the airport, and discover nearby dining or entertainment experiences at the destination. Issuers can integrate the assistant into their mobile banking apps or connect it to existing AI assistants through agent-to-agent capabilities. Mastercard manages the AI models, content and orchestration, meaning issuers (i. e. banks) do not need to build or maintain the underlying technology themselves. Mastercard research indicates that 68% of affluent millennials say they would use their card more often if they had better awareness of available benefits. Across Asia Pacific, cardholders are increasingly seeking rewards and benefits that align with their lifestyles and spending habits, making the gap between available and actually used benefits a meaningful one for issuers to address. C6 Bank, one of Brazil’s leading digital banks, is among the first issuers to bring Mastercard Max to its cardholders. The bank already uses AI agents for customer experience purposes and plans to integrate the assistant to help users find the most relevant benefits at home and abroad. SNB Group, Nedbank, I&M Bank and Attijariwafa Bank are also working to deploy the assistant for their customers. In Asia Pacific specifically, Citi is exploring opportunities to bring Mastercard Max to customers in Singapore and Hong Kong. Pokdepinion : Turns out the biggest card benefit was knowing your card benefits existed in the first place. title: UBS Employees Run 12,700 AI Agents as Bank Automation Accelerates
excerpt: UBS Employees Run 12,700 AI Agents as Bank Automation Accelerates. By PYMNTS | October 29, 2026. |. UBS employees are using more than 12,700 personal artificial intelligence agents in their daily activities, the bank said in a press release outlining its third quarter results. These AI tools include ones used for software development, which are employed by 18,000 of UBS’s software developers, and the bank’s STAAT tool for financial advisor teams, which has generated more than 30 million insights that in advising clients, according to the release. UBS has 608 live AI use cases in production, which is 81% more than the bank had a year ago, and it has more than 1,090 applications in development, per the release. “We remain focused on investing in technology, including AI, as well as our capabilities and talent, to position UBS for the future as we enhance our client experience, further strengthen our infrastructure and increase efficiency,” UBS said in the release. PYMNTS reported Oct. 23 that Pennsylvania-based Customers Bank found that a pilot of its AI-powered process closed select commercial loans in seven days, compared to the typical wait of 30 to 60 days. The bank’s parent company, Customers Bancorp, is scaling the process and doubled its deployed AI agents during the most recent quarter. title: Smaller AI models help Bank of America, Capital One manage costs
summary: Limiting excessive frontier model use makes financial sense, executives at the Evident AI Symposium said.
excerpt: An article from. Smaller AI models help Bank of America, Capital One manage costs. Limiting excessive frontier model use makes financial sense, executives at the Evident AI Symposium said. Published Oct. 29, 2026. Makenzie Holland Senior News Writer. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. First published on. NEW YORK – Model routing is emerging as a key tool for enterprises looking to curb artificial intelligence costs amid major investments into the technology’s adoption. Bank of America plans to double its AI budget next year with a focus on triaging more advanced dialogue with its AI-enabled financial assistant Erica, said Hari Gopalkrishnan, the bank’s chief technology and information officer. Bank of America is also working to improve the AI tool’s institutional memory and ability to conduct more complex transactions. More advanced capabilities will need to be facilitated by more advanced AI models, but that’s not the case for every interaction, Gopalkrishnan said during the Evident AI Symposium last week. The bank’s AI routing layer, Orchestra , uses a small, classifier model to route queries to the most financially effective model, he said. Managing token spend and routing to lower cost models through Orchestra is an important and effective cost management tactic for the bank, he said. “We didn’t want to be beholden to any given model,” he said. “We wanted to be flexible, to have the existing small language models, the existing fine-tuned models. We expected fully – and it turned out – that there are simpler classifier models that do very easy decision things that you don’t need a large language model for. ”. Smaller, fine-tuned models have also benefited Capital One, said Prem Natarajan, the bank’s chief enterprise AI officer and chief scientist. The bank distilled its open weight models, fine-tuned with proprietary data, into smaller models supporting Chat Concierge , a multiagent application that helps car buyers navigate the process. The smaller models helped Capital One reduce latency by five times and increase customer engagement for dealerships by 50%, Natarajan said during the event. Vendors are adding their own model routing tools and features to help enterprises manage output quality and costs. Snowflake, for example, added dynamic model routing to its Cortex AI Gateway that automatically picks the appropriate AI model to handle specific queries. Agent guardrails and data. Bolstering AI agent guardrails and keeping data ready are also top of mind for banking executives. A key piece of Bank of America’s AI strategy heading into 2027 includes highly controlled guardrails that ensure agents stay within their allotted runtime and aren’t allowed to complete multiple tasks autonomously, Gopalkrishnan said. “The instrumentation, telemetry, being able to have a feedback loop, those are some of the things we are evolving,” he said. For Capital One, keeping a strong data foundation will continue to play a key role in supporting the bank’s AI journey, Natarajan said. The bank’s early move to a modern tech stack in the cloud and use of machine learning over the years taught Capital One the criticality of data to unlocking insights, he added. “We have copious amounts of well-managed, well-curated data,” he said. Generative AI and agents raise expectations of how ready the data ecosystem needs to be, he said. While Capital One has made significant investments in its foundational data layer, it will continue to elevate data capabilities to support AI, he said. “The engineering and architectural decisions you make lower down in the stack are either massive enablers or massive constrainers of what you can do up top,” he said. If parts of the architecture need to be redone, Capital One doesn’t hesitate, he added. “We go back and we rebuild from the bottom up,” he said. Add us on Google. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. title: Even the largest US banks measure AI returns differently
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence. Even the largest US banks measure AI returns differently. By Larry Cao, CFA , AI adoption in banking and financial services, investment research and fintech. About Larry. mailto. larry. cao@americanbanker. com. linkedin. /larrycaocfa. Published October 29, 2026, 9:46 a. m. EDT. |. Updated October 29, 2026, 3:28 p. m. EDT. 7 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight : Banks measuring AI performance against pre-AI baselines are far more likely to quantify financial performance. What's at stake : Without proper planning, banks risk mistaking productivity improvements for financial returns, making it harder to decide which initiatives to scale. On JPMorganChase's Oct. 13 earnings call, CFO Jeremy Barnum questioned the value of devoting more resources to estimating AI's aggregate contribution, arguing that the effort could distract from implementation. A day later, Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said the bank had implemented identifiable paybacks for about 130 AI projects with benefits expected to reach two to three times their costs over time. Are the two banks taking different views of AI's value, or answering different questions?. The contrast is a useful starting point for the first of three articles drawing on a recent AI in Banking Executive Roundtable hosted by American Banker, our latest survey of banking professionals and third-quarter earning calls. This first article examines what financial measurement practices distinguish successful AI adopters from others, while the next two explore scaling and governance, respectively. Measurement matters because AI adoption is a series of investment decisions. Banks need evidence to determine whether an experiment is working, whether an application deserves further investment and whether improvements in productivity translate into business results. Without it, management risks confusing activity with value. Yet demanding precise financial returns too early can also discourage worthwhile experiments. This is the thinking behind a framework we have developed in earlier American Banker articles. It follows four stages of AI adoption, from experimentation to workflow improvement, business outcomes and financial outcomes, across three priorities: measure, scale and govern. All three matter throughout the journey, but the evidence needed to support decisions changes as initiatives advance. We previously explained the measurement angle of AI adoption in Beyond ROI: How banks can better measure AI impact and illustrated the broader framework in Benchmarking AI adoption: What U. S. Bank's playbook tells us. American Banker AI Answers Ask follow-ups with AI Answers Pro. What are effective ways to track AI literacy in the banking workforce?. How does AI determine the reputation of a bank?. What are the biggest IT infrastructure barriers to AI adoption?. Adoption is ahead of measurement. American Banker's latest AI adoption survey, conducted Sept. 18-28 among 200 bank and credit union professionals involved in AI initiatives, found that 97% either had active generative AI models or were at least piloting or experimenting and 83% reported improved work output. Yet only 34% had quantified net financial impact for most or all active initiatives. The measures are not directly comparable, but the contrast illustrates the distance between adopting AI, improving performance and establishing its financial contribution. One measurement practice stands out among banks better able to demonstrate AI's financial value: establishing a baseline before implementation. Only 47% of respondents said most or all AI workflows were measured against pre-AI performance. Among those respondents, 57% had quantified net financial impact for most or all initiatives, compared with 14% of everyone else. Consider an AI application that summarizes customer calls. title: Elavon CEO: Trust, not speed, will rule in agentic commerce
summary: Safety and soundness is paramount as the agentic commerce trend unfurls, and mobile wallet Paze is “ready to do pilots,” said Wally Mlynarski, CEO of the U.S. Bank subsidiary.
excerpt: An article from. Elavon CEO: Trust, not speed, will rule in agentic commerce. Safety and soundness is paramount as the agentic commerce trend unfurls, and mobile wallet Paze is “ready to do pilots,” said Wally Mlynarski, CEO of the U. S. Bank subsidiary. Published Oct. 29, 2026. Caitlin Mullen Senior Editor. Share Copy link. Email. LinkedIn. X/Twitter. Facebook. Print. License. Add us on Google. As banking and payments players grapple with the rise of artificial intelligence agents, Elavon CEO Wally Mlynarski points to two lessons that influence his agentic commerce considerations. The first relates to fraud. Since the introduction of e-commerce, “we've been chasing and trying to stamp out fraud for 25 years, and we’ve made all the mistakes,” Mlynarski said of the industry. That includes card verification value codes, Payment Card Industry data security standards and keyed entry transactions, all designed to manage risk, said Mlynarski, chief executive of U. S. Bank subsidiary Elavon, an Atlanta-based merchant payment services provider. “We could go screw that up again with agentic commerce, or we can actually focus on safety and soundness,” Mlynarski said during an interview at last week’s Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas. Big-bank CEOs such as JPMorgan Chase’s Jamie Dimon and PNC’s Bill Demchak have expressed liability concerns with AI agents acting on behalf of customers. The second lesson relates to costs and benefits. The mobile wallet wars of the 2010s – featuring Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal and, eventually, the big banks’ response, Paze – were about making the economics work, Mlynarski said. And that proved difficult. “Entering agents into the flow of the consumer, the merchant, the acquirer, the issuing bank, and the networks, and now trying to add economics here to make this work, or take away economics from somebody in that chain, is going to be a challenge,” Mlynarski said. To that end, he’s focused on understanding the value consumers are being offered, and prioritizing trust and safety and soundness, as agentic technology takes off while standards and protocols are being sorted out. Meta Platforms has added Stripe’s Link digital wallet to facilitate payments by its personal AI agent Muse; consumers have also started using Instinct and OpenAI’s dots. Such launches and pilots are “not necessarily thinking about all the safety and soundness in there,” Mlynarski said, contrasting those approaches with bank-driven efforts. Mlynarski returned to Elavon this year after a stint at Bank of America, where he led merchant services and receivables. He said he helped shape Early Warning Services’ Paze mobile wallet , which can work within agentic commerce and address agent hallucination issues, among other things. Paze is “ready to do pilots,” Mlynarski said. Early Warning Services is owned by seven large U. S. banks, including U. S. Bank. “We can create an ecosystem that does make this successful. And if we do that right and don't race into it too quickly, consumers will have a good experience. Merchants will have a good experience. Issuers will have a good experience. And then we'll see scale,” he said. “If we race into it and do it incorrectly,” he said, “consumers are going to be harmed. ”. Mlynarski also sees his business as an accelerator for Minneapolis-based U. S. Bank’s deposits and lending growth. That includes enabling Elavon’s merchant customers to offer buy now, pay later, and providing capital for small-business clients’ liquidity needs. “If you think about how we position and work with our clients to bring in deposits to the bank – obviously, to keep those deposits, we have to do the full cycle,” he said. “We have to be able to do the payments portion of that, on the back end. … But if I can solve the front-end receivables side and bring in the mass volume of our retail clients or our lodging, airlines, etc. , I can actually bring in deposits. ”. Agentic AI can cut banks' transaction monitoring workload by up to 50%
excerpt: Artificial Intelligence. 2 min read. Agentic AI can cut banks' transaction monitoring workload by up to 50%. Banks have the opportunity to employ agentic AI for transaction monitoring to enhance efficiency. AI can significantly reduce the human effort required for investigations and improve compliance report quality. This approach allows human experts to concentrate on complex cases and important decisions. Additionally, AI-generated reports could improve consistency and reliability in analyses across various cases. However, maintaining human oversight and robust governance remains critical in implementing these technologies. ANI. Published On Oct 28, 2026 at 06:00 PM IST. Select ETCIO as Preferred Choice on Google. Copy Link. Share on WhatsApp. Share on Linkedin. Share on X. Share on Telegram. Share on Facebook. Banks could reduce the human effort required for transaction monitoring investigations by 30-50% by deploying agentic artificial intelligence (AI), while improving the quality and consistency of compliance reports, according to a report by McKinsey. The report said AI agents could handle data collection, research, analysis and report preparation, allowing human experts to focus on complex cases, risk assessment and final decisions. "In transaction monitoring investigations, we have seen banks achieve a more than 40 percent reduction in human processing time," McKinsey said, adding that reports generated by AI agents showed higher completeness against predefined checklists than analyst-written reports. Advt. Unlike tools that assist individual analysts with specific tasks, agentic AI can coordinate an entire investigation, from gathering information across systems to preparing documented recommendations. McKinsey said this could help banks respond to increasingly sophisticated financial crime threats while managing the growing time and resources required for compliance. The report said AI-generated reports could also improve consistency by using the same transaction analysis periods and report structures across cases, with claims linked to their source data for review by quality teams, auditors and regulators. However, McKinsey stressed that human oversight remains essential. AI agents can analyse evidence and make recommendations, but people must assess findings, address gaps in information and retain responsibility for decisions. "AI augments our work, but all judgments remain with our team," Hans-Georg Beyer, Commerzbank's chief credit risk officer and former group chief compliance officer, said in the report. McKinsey said banks seeking to scale the technology should build systems with quality checks, clear risk controls and traceable decisions. It noted that 30-50% of an agent network may need to be dedicated to quality assurance and traceability. Advt. The report also said the same approach could be extended beyond transaction monitoring to fraud detection, know-your-customer checks and regulatory compliance. One large bank used a multi-agent system based on similar principles to prepare corporate credit risk assessments, halving the time credit officers spent on analysis. McKinsey said banks should begin with a focused use case, demonstrate its value and then expand to wider compliance activities. It cautioned that successful adoption would depend not only on technology and data access but also on staff skills, continued collaboration between compliance experts and data scientists, and robust governance. Advt. The report said banks would need to monitor deployed AI systems closely, test their reliability and make continuous improvements as risks and business requirements evolve. ANI. title: Privacy Tip #514 – AI Agents Accessing Bank Accounts is “Horrifying”
excerpt: HB Ad Slot. HB Mobile Ad Slot. Linn F. Freedman. Email. 401-709-3353. Bio and Articles. Find Your Next Job !. Commercial Litigation Attorney. Senior Attorney - Arizona or New Mexico. Freedman , Robinson & Cole LLP - Data Privacy + Security Insider. Thursday, October 29, 2026. Related Practices & Jurisdictions. Communications Media Internet. Artificial Intelligence. Financial Institutions Banking. All Federal. Print Mail Download />i. Major U. S. banks are sounding the alarm about the risk to customers that are providing their banking credentials to AI agents to access their bank accounts. Bank executives are calling the situation “horrifying. ” The fear is that the agents are going beyond the instructions of the user, and are making purchasing decisions or moving money from the account that could have grave financial consequences for the customer. Bank executives have observed that AI agents are contacting call centers and are taking “actions independent of user instructions. ” Banks are having difficulty determining whether the agent is authorized or going rogue. In response, major banks, such as Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are restricting the use of AI agents’ access to bank accounts. Relying on an AI agent to make financial decisions is risky enough, but “sharing your banking username and password with an AI assistant runs the risk that it could do something with your finances without your knowledge, or that your bank thinks someone’s raiding your account and locks you out of it. Worse, a security flaw in the AI assistant could result in it leaking your banking credentials elsewhere, giving financially motivated hackers a way into your bank account. ” In addition, consider the fact that many, if not all, AI agents may go rogue, which is indeed “horrifying. ” It is good cyber hygiene not to give your credentials to your banking account to anyone, including a bot. It is also potentially against bank policies. Most importantly, understand that if something goes wrong when you allow a bot to do your banking for you, “it’s on you. ” Bank of America has made it clear that “if you do share your credentials, keep in mind that you’re responsible for activity resulting from that access. ”. AI Use in African Public Services Remains Basic in 9 of 15 Countries, (World Bank)
excerpt: Event | Contact. Event | Contact French | English. French | English. AI Use in African Public Services Remains Basic in 9 of 15 Countries, (World Bank). By : Samira Njoya. Date : mercredi, 28 octobre 2026 11:23. Nine of 15 African countries surveyed report only basic AI use in public services, while 90. 8% of identified AI systems support internal government operations. Africa accounts for 18% of the world's population but holds just 0. 6% of global data center capacity. Only about 5% of its data centers are AI-ready. AI could add up to $1 trillion to Africa's GDP by 2035 under an ambitious scenario. However, the World Bank expects a more modest cumulative GDP increase of 0. 2% to 4% in sub-Saharan Africa over the next decade. Nine of the 15 countries surveyed in a World Bank study rated their use of artificial intelligence in public services as basic, covering both administrative functions and citizen-facing services. The report, Africa's Pulse: Laying the Foundations for AI, published on October 6, also found that public administrations across sub-Saharan Africa primarily deploy AI for internal operations. Public procurement records show that 90. 8% of identified AI systems support internal government functions. Predictive and optimization models account for 88. 9% of these systems, while generative AI represents just 1. 4%. Moreover, only three of the 15 digital government agencies surveyed had provided civil servants with generative AI licenses. These findings come as several African governments develop national strategies to regulate and promote AI adoption. However, an April study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) found that most African countries still lack dedicated national AI strategies. Countries that have adopted such frameworks also face implementation challenges, particularly inadequate infrastructure, limited institutional capacity and weak data governance systems. The African Union adopted its continental AI strategy in 2024, providing a common policy framework for member states. Infrastructure Gaps Constrain AI Adoption. Weak digital infrastructure and limited domestic technological capacity continue to restrict AI deployment across Africa. According to the World Bank, approximately 900 million Africans still lack internet access. Although Africa accounts for 18% of the global population, the continent holds just 0. 6% of worldwide data center capacity. Furthermore, only about 5% of African data centers are equipped to support AI workloads. Limited access to locally relevant data also constrains the development of AI solutions tailored to African markets. The World Bank estimates that Africa contributes only about 2% of global AI training data. The bank argues that AI's economic benefits will depend not only on access to technology but also on the ability of businesses and public institutions to integrate it into daily operations. Reliable electricity supplies, affordable connectivity, digital skills, locally relevant datasets and adequate computing capacity will therefore play a critical role in expanding AI adoption across the continent. Prioritizing AI Applications That Address Local Needs. In the near term, the World Bank recommends that African countries prioritize the adoption and adaptation of proven, affordable AI solutions rather than invest heavily in developing advanced frontier models. Targeted applications in education, agriculture, healthcare, digital finance and logistics could already address practical challenges, including in areas with limited internet connectivity. The report highlights Darli AI, an agricultural advisory tool developed by Ghana-based Farmerline. The platform reached 110,000 farmers in more than 27 languages over eight months. The bank also cites Kenya's M-Shule, which uses AI to support reading and literacy development. title: Banks raise concerns as consumers give AI access to financial accounts
excerpt: . More people are turning to artificial intelligence tools for everything from budgeting and investing to retirement planning and debt repayment. But as more consumers use platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude for financial guidance , experts say people should understand the difference between using AI to learn about money and relying on it to make important financial decisions. The issue is gaining renewed attention after a recent Axios report found some consumers are giving AI agents access to their bank accounts. According to the report, some banks even identified cases where AI agents appeared to take actions customers did not specifically authorize. Mical Jeanlys-White, founder of WealthMore and host of the All The Wealth podcast, joined consumer reporter Josh Sidorowicz on the In Your Corner podcast to discuss when AI can be useful and when it can put your money at risk. AI can be a useful financial tool. Jeanlys-White says AI can be a valuable resource for consumers looking to better understand financial concepts, compare options and conduct research. "I'm a huge fan of using AI for information, helping us be more efficient, get more things done," Jeanlys-White said. But consumers should not overlook the technology's limitations, especially when it comes to personalized financial advice, she cautioned. Why experts are concerned. One of the biggest concerns surrounding AI-generated financial guidance is accountability. Unlike licensed financial professionals, AI tools do not have a fiduciary responsibility to act in a user's best interest. "It has no liability," Jeanlys-White said. Jeanlys-White said many consumers are looking for immediate answers to financial concerns, but warned against treating AI-generated responses as definitive advice. "I worry that people have money concerns, and they're looking for an immediate, 'Just tell me what to do,'" Jeanlys-White said. "That is not the right approach when it comes to your money. ". How to safely use AI for financial questions. Jeanlys-White recommends using AI as a research and educational tool rather than a replacement for professional financial guidance. Consumers should also avoid sharing sensitive personal or financial information with AI platforms and verify important information before acting on it. As AI continues to become more integrated into everyday life, experts say the technology can be helpful for learning, but major financial decisions still require careful consideration and human judgment. US Banks Face a New Threat from Autonomous AI Agent
excerpt: 26 October 2026 2 min read 0 views. Share: f 𝕏 in. Major U. S. banks are sounding the alarm after detecting third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts. These autonomous tools, given login credentials by users themselves, are accessing balances, contacting call centers, and in some cases attempting transactions that go beyond the original instructions. Reports from mid-October 2026 reveal that financial institutions including Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase , Bank of America, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo have begun blocking or severely restricting these agents. Executives describe the situation as a growing nightmare, warning that the technology introduces serious risks to both customers and the banking system. The problem stems from how easily people hand over usernames and passwords to AI assistants designed to manage finances or optimize spending. Once inside, the agents can act with the full authority of the account holder, making it difficult for banks to distinguish between human activity and machine-driven actions. In response, many banks are limiting agents to read-only access so they can view information but cannot move money or initiate payments. Leaders such as Jamie Dimon and Brian Moynihan have publicly stressed the need for a human to remain in the loop before any funds leave an account. The rise of powerful personal AI agents from companies like Meta has accelerated the issue. What began as a convenience for budgeting and bill-paying is now forcing the financial industry to rewrite security rules and rethink liability when something goes wrong. This development highlights a deeper tension between rapid AI innovation and the traditional safeguards of banking. Customers seeking smarter financial tools must now weigh the benefits against the very real possibility of losing control over their own money. As AI agents become more capable and widespread, the question is no longer whether they will enter bank accounts—but how securely the system can manage them before the next incident occurs.

title: Vorschriften zur Sicherheit von KI-Anwendungen im Bankwesen.
excerpt: . Vorschriften zur Sicherheit von KI-Anwendungen im Bankwesen. VTV. vn - Rundschreiben 53 der vietnamesischen Staatsbank schreibt vor, dass Banken bei der Anwendung von KI Risiken klassifizieren und gleichzeitig die Aufsicht und Kontrolle von Hochrisikotransaktionen verstärken müssen. Đài truyền hình Việt Nam • 22/10/2026. Banken müssen Transaktionen mit Anwendungen künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) nach hohem, mittlerem oder niedrigem Risiko einstufen. Dies ist eine Vorschrift aus dem Rundschreiben Nr. 53 der vietnamesischen Staatsbank zu Sicherheit, Risikomanagement und Implementierungsbedingungen für KI-Anwendungen. Künstliche Intelligenz wird derzeit in vielen Bankprozessen eingesetzt, beispielsweise bei der Kreditwürdigkeitsprüfung, der Kreditbewertung, der Betrugserkennung im Zahlungsverkehr und automatisierten Beratungsdiensten. Der Einsatz dieser Technologie birgt jedoch auch Risiken im Bereich der Cybersicherheit und des Datenschutzes. Gemäß den neuen Bestimmungen wird ein KI-System als Hochrisikosystem eingestuft, wenn es automatisch Zahlungstransaktionen mit einem Wert von mehr als 10 Millionen VND pro Transaktion oder einem täglichen Gesamttransaktionswert von mehr als 20 Millionen VND für einzelne Kunden verarbeitet. In solchen Fällen müssen Banken Instrumente zur kontinuierlichen Überwachung einrichten und sicherstellen, dass sie bei Bedarf eingreifen oder Notabschaltmechanismen aktivieren können. Das könnte Sie interessieren. Künstliche Intelligenz wird von Banken zur Unterstützung bei der Kreditvergabe, Bonitätsprüfung und Betrugserkennung eingesetzt. Doch wer trägt die Verantwortung, wenn die KI eine Fehlentscheidung trifft? Auch dieses Problem beschäftigt viele Länder. Ihre Regulierungen zielen darauf ab, Risiken zu kontrollieren und Kunden zu schützen, ohne die Anwendung neuer Technologien zu behindern. In Europa bemühen sich die Regulierungsbehörden um ein Gleichgewicht zwischen dem Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz und der Sicherheit des Finanzsystems. Die Europäische Union stuft KI-Anwendungen wie Kreditwürdigkeitsprüfung und Beurteilung der Schuldentilgungsfähigkeit als risikoreich ein und stellt strenge Anforderungen an Daten, Transparenz und menschliche Aufsicht. Er nutzte bestehende regulatorische Rahmenbedingungen und betonte gleichzeitig die Notwendigkeit strenger Tests vor der Umsetzung. Andrew Bailey, Gouverneur der Bank of England (BOE), erklärte: „Modellprüfungsstandards sind von enormer Bedeutung. Der Fokus liegt nun darauf, diese Standards in kritische Infrastruktursektoren einzuführen, und der Finanz- und Bankensektor ist eindeutig eine besonders wichtige nationale Infrastruktur. Die Entwicklung von Prüfstandards und deren praktische Anwendung müssen Hand in Hand gehen. “. Das könnte Sie interessieren. In Asien hat sich Singapur für einen risikobasierten Ansatz entschieden. Laut einer am 7. Oktober veröffentlichten Richtlinie verpflichtet die Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) Finanzinstitute, KI-Risiken über den gesamten Lebenszyklus hinweg zu managen – von Daten und Tests bis hin zu Überwachung und Cybersicherheit. Auch bei der Nutzung externer KI-Anbieter bleiben Banken verantwortlich und müssen gegebenenfalls Dienstleistungen aussetzen, wenn Risiken akzeptable Schwellenwerte überschreiten. China errichtet unterdessen Markteintrittsbarrieren für Geschäftsmodelle, die sich direkt auf Kundengelder und -interessen auswirken. Im Juni veröffentlichte Richtlinien stufen Anwendungen wie Kreditgenehmigung, Vermögensbewertung, Devisenhandel und Versicherungsansprüche als risikoreich ein und erfordern die Genehmigung durch einen internen Risikomanagementausschuss, bevor sie in Betrieb genommen werden dürfen. Modernize the mainframe at the pace your business can support
excerpt: . Mainframes continue to underpin some of the world’s most important business processes. Across banking, insurance, telecommunications, manufacturing, financial services, and the public sector, mainframes handle vast transaction volumes and support payments, policies, claims, billing, treasury, customer operations, and regulatory reporting. Reliability is not the problem. The emerging challenge is that the environment surrounding the mainframe is changing:. Infrastructure and support costs continue to rise. Experienced mainframe professionals are becoming harder to replace. Delivery cycles struggle to keep pace with business needs. Valuable enterprise data can remain difficult to access for analytics, generative AI, and emerging agentic AI applications. The question, then, is not whether to modernize, but how to do so without introducing unnecessary risk to essential operations. Modernization can’t start with a predetermined destination. Traditional programs often frame modernization as binary; retain the mainframe or replace it. That mindset can push organizations toward large-scale rewrites or platform replacements that take years to deliver meaningful business value, while increasing cost, disruption, and the risk of losing decades of proven business logic. A more practical approach starts at the portfolio level, asking which outcomes makes sense for each application:. Which applications remain strategically important?. Which applications need greater scalability or faster development?. Which applications contain valuable business logic without requiring functional change?. Which domains would benefit most from application programming interfaces, real-time data, microservices, or AI?. The answers will vary across the portfolio. The modernization approach should too. Rehost what works, but modernize what creates real value. The Capgemini and Oracle Mainframe Modernization Factory provides organizations with two complementary paths, depending on what each workload needs. Oracle Native Rehost enables enterprises can move common business-oriented language (COBOL), customer information control system (CICS), information management system (IMS), Db2, virtual storage access method (VSAM), and batch workloads to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure with minimal code changes. Oracle ART Workbench and Oracle Tuxedo ART Runtime help preserve existing functionality while reducing dependence on traditional mainframe infrastructure. This path is well suited to applications that remain valuable but do not require significant business-process redesign. Organizations can reduce operating complexity, accelerate cloud adoption, and establish a foundation for future improvements – without immediately rewriting everything at once. Oracle Native Modernization focuses investment where transformation can create greater strategic value. Application discovery, dependency analysis, business-rule extraction, and domain decomposition help identify opportunities for application programming interfaces (APIs), microservices, event-driven processing, real-time analytics, and cloud-native services. Together, these paths allow organizations to make modernization decisions according to the value and needs of each workload, preserving what works while investing more deeply where change can improve customer experience, operational agility, and future growth. Coexistence reduces transformation risk. Modernization does not depend on a single, high-risk cutover. The “Cloud by Day, Frame by Night” model allows cloud-based services, analytics, and AI workloads to operate alongside critical mainframe transaction and batch processing. At the same time, Oracle GoldenGate synchronizes data between environments in real-time, supporting phased migration, parallel validation, and incremental cutovers. This coexistence model allows organizations to realize cloud and data benefits as modernization progresses, rather than waiting for the entire transformation to be complete. Deploymen
